title: One of His Codes Got Cracked. This One Never Has.
standfirst: Marsden Hartley spent two years turning a dead lieutenant's regiment number, age and initials into paint, and scholars eventually read every mark. The letters in this picture, made the same year he came home from that war, have never been explained.

sections.heading: A Grief Written in Numbers
sections.body: In Berlin in 1914, months after his closest friend was killed at the front, Hartley painted a memorial with no face in it. *Portrait of a German Officer* arranges flags, medals and fragments of a uniform into something closer to a coat of arms than a likeness: the German Empire's black-white-red flag and Bavaria's blue-and-white check at the bottom, an Iron Cross at the top, a white-striped officer's epaulette, and — set into the paint like initials cut into silver — the letters and numbers scholars have since read as a private obituary. A monogram in [gold-on-red lettering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portrait_of_a_German_Officer) reads K.v.F. The number 24 was the age at which his friend died. The number 4 was that friend's regiment, and, [by one museum's reading](https://wam.umn.edu/marsden-hartley-portrait-1914-15), also the number of the house Hartley was living in when he painted it. Even the war's other side gets a line in the code: the English Cross of St George and the [Belgian tricolour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portrait_of_a_German_Officer), tucked in at the bottom, naming the enemy his friend had been sent to fight.

sections.heading: The Lieutenant Under the Numbers
sections.body: Karl von Freyburg was born in Flensburg on 15 July 1889, the only son of a major in the Prussian army. He trained at the cadet academy in Berlin-Lichterfelde and was [commissioned lieutenant](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_von_Freyburg) in the 4th Guard Regiment on Foot in 1908. He and Hartley did not meet in Berlin at all — they met in Paris, in 1912, introduced by von Freyburg's cousin, the sculptor Arnold Rönnebeck. Whatever passed between the two men over the following two years, Hartley's own account of it reads as more than friendship, and most scholars now take the coded paintings as confirmation enough. Von Freyburg had received the Iron Cross shortly before his death; on 7 October 1914, in the opening battles of the war, he was [killed at Gommecourt](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_von_Freyburg), in the Pas-de-Calais, and buried in the German military cemetery at Neuville-Saint-Vaast — a war his own portrait would go on fighting, in code, for a New York audience that had no idea who he was.

sections.heading: The Painter Who Went Looking for Him
sections.body: Hartley was born Edmund Hartley in Lewiston, Maine, on 4 January 1877, the youngest of nine children; his mother died when he was eight. He trained conventionally enough in New York, under William Merritt Chase, before Europe rearranged his sense of what painting was for. He reached Paris in 1912 and fell in with Gertrude Stein's circle; Berlin, the following year, changed him further. There he found Wassily Kandinsky and Franz Marc's circle — the loose group later known as [Der Blaue Reiter](https://unframed.lacma.org/node/1421) — more useful to him than anything Paris had shown him, and began painting the pageantry of his adopted city, its parades and uniforms, with something like the seriousness Marc gave to horses. When von Freyburg died, that vocabulary — flags, insignia, the shorthand of military display — was the only one Hartley had left for grief, and he kept working in it for the best part of a year.

sections.heading: Home, and Not Welcome
sections.body: The war that killed von Freyburg eventually made Berlin impossible for an American to stay in, and Hartley returned to the United States in early 1916, at close to the worst possible moment to be seen carrying German imagery — [anti-German feeling](https://www.dailyartmagazine.com/marsden-hartley-an-overlooked-modernist/) in New York was near its peak, a year before the country itself entered the war. Hartley and his German-inflected work were, in the years that followed, [treated with suspicion](https://www.dailyartmagazine.com/marsden-hartley-an-overlooked-modernist/) as sympathetic to a cause America had just finished fighting, and it took decades for critics to separate the private mourning inside the pictures from the public symbol on their surface. *Portrait of a German Officer* is now often described as [one of the first](https://www.dailyartmagazine.com/marsden-hartley-an-overlooked-modernist/) works in modern American art built around openly queer desire, hidden inside a perfectly conventional military portrait — a reading nobody in 1916 was in any position to make.

sections.heading: A Second Set of Letters
sections.body: That same year, back in New York, Hartley painted a glass of green absinthe. *Handsome Drinks* keeps faith with the café culture he had absorbed in Paris, but it also keeps faith with the coding habit Berlin had taught him: flattened shapes sit next to lettering that looks, in the manner of Cubist collage, as though it had been [pasted onto the surface](https://www.flickr.com/photos/gandalfsgallery/50070428023) from somewhere else, while other letters sit inside the illusion of the room as if they were objects on the table. What the letters spell, or stand for, nobody has worked out. The record calls them simply [mysterious](https://www.sartle.com/artwork/handsome-drinks-marsden-hartley) — personal to Hartley, and never explained by him, in an exhibition statement or anywhere else. It sits oddly next to *Portrait of a German Officer*: one code that took scholars decades to break, and a second, smaller one, made the same year, that has defeated everybody who has tried.

sections.heading: Nobody Has Agreed on Him Either
sections.body: Hartley's reputation never settled either. Reviewing his career in 1947, four years after his death, the dealer Hudson Walker wrote that opinions on the painter ran to extremes and always had — [some critics maintained](https://daily.jstor.org/was-marsden-hartley-really-a-great-painter) flatly that he did not know how to paint, others ranked him with Winslow Homer for sheer originality. He never explained the letters in *Handsome Drinks*, any more than he explained, in his own lifetime, exactly what Karl von Freyburg had meant to him. The nearest he came to it was decades later and obliquely, in the frank [male nudes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marsden_Hartley) of his final years — paintings, made around 1940, that for the first time didn't need a code at all.
